physics-killer-07.material: As observed from Earth, a star is $6$ light-years away. A spaceship leaves Earth for the star at a constant speed of $0.6c$ and arrives at the star. Which option correctly gives, in order, the flight time measured by an observer on Earth and the flight time measured by a clock aboard the spaceship? (Take the speed of light $c$ as $1$ light-year per year.)
physics-killer-07.thinking.0: Newton's Laws of Motion and Special Relativity
physics-killer-07.s.s1.prompt: As observed from Earth, a star is $6$ light-years away. A spaceship leaves Earth for the star at a constant speed of $0.6c$ and arrives at the star. Which option correctly gives, in order, the flight time measured by an observer on Earth and the flight time measured by a clock aboard the spaceship? (Take the speed of light $c$ as $1$ light-year per year.)
physics-killer-07.s.s1.explain: Earth observer: $\Delta t=\dfrac{6\text{ light-years}}{0.6c}=10$ years. $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-0.6^2}=1/0.8=1.25$. The ship's clock is present at both departure and arrival, so it measures the proper time: $\Delta t_0=\Delta t/\gamma=10/1.25=8$ years. Multiplying gives $12.5$ years (option 3), dividing by $\gamma^2$ gives $6.4$ years (option 1), and swapping the two values gives option 4. (In the ship's frame the distance is contracted to $6/1.25=4.8$ light-years, and $4.8/0.6=8$ years, in agreement.)
